strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-served problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction for fisheye and 360-degree imagery, where pinhole-trained foundation models often fail. This is a meaningful computer vision contribution with clear practical relevance for robotics, AR/VR, mapping, and egocentric/omnidirectional capture.

The proposed formulation is sensible: decomposing point-map prediction into ray direction and radial distance, using spherical-harmonic ray representations, and adding camera-model conditioning are well aligned with the geometry of wide-FoV cameras. The method also builds naturally on strong recent feed-forward reconstruction models rather than inventing unnecessary machinery.

The empirical results are broad and generally convincing. The paper evaluates pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, large-scale localization, and monocular 360 depth across fisheye and spherical datasets. The reported gains over VGGT and pi3 on Stanford2D3D and other wide-FoV settings are large, and the qualitative results support the claim that distortion-aware modeling improves robustness.

The paper includes useful ablations on camera-model tokens, training data composition, and number of frames per batch. The finding that diverse camera-model training improves 360-degree performance despite limited 360 supervision is interesting and practically useful.

The method has a strong efficiency argument in large-scale localization: although it does not always match the best SfM-based accuracy, it registers all images in the reported Matterport3D scenes and runs in seconds rather than minutes, which is a meaningful systems-level advantage.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level. The architecture appears to combine pi3-style permutation-equivariant multi-view reconstruction with UniK3D-style spherical-harmonic ray modeling and camera-conditioning ideas. The resulting system is valuable, but the paper should be more precise about what is technically new beyond this integration.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. In particular, claims of being the first feed-forward multi-view wide-FoV reconstruction foundation model may be plausible, but the comparison table simplifies related work and does not deeply discuss systems that use omnidirectional SfM, dense matching, or wide-FoV depth priors in multi-view pipelines.

The fairness of the baseline comparison is a concern. VGGT and pi3 are evaluated largely as pinhole-oriented zero-shot baselines, while Wid3R is explicitly trained with wide-FoV data and augmentations. This is a relevant practical comparison, but it does not isolate whether the gains come from the proposed camera representation, the added wide-FoV training data, or both. Fine-tuned or data-matched baselines would strengthen the case.

The method description lacks some reproducibility details. It is unclear how camera tokens are assigned in ambiguous cases, how much camera-type knowledge is required at inference, how intrinsics variation within a camera class is handled, how ground-truth rays are obtained for all datasets, and whether the model generalizes to unseen fisheye/omnidirectional calibration parameters rather than only known dataset distributions.

Some evaluations are potentially confounded by dataset overlap or in-distribution testing. The model is trained on datasets including Matterport3D and ScanNet++, and later evaluated on their official test splits. This is legitimate if splits are disjoint, but the paper should more explicitly separate zero-shot cross-dataset claims from in-dataset generalization and report whether scenes, buildings, or camera rigs overlap.

The monocular 360 depth comparison is mixed. Wid3R achieves strong threshold accuracy, but its AbsRel is worse than several task-specific 360 depth models trained directly on Matterport3D. The text describes the result as comparable or superior, which is only partially true depending on the metric.

The ablation study is helpful but not complete. It does not separately ablate the angular/radial decomposition, spherical harmonics versus a direct ray head, camera-token alternatives, or the effect of initializing from pi3. These would better establish which design choices are essential.

Limitations are underdeveloped. Dynamic scenes are mentioned, but other important limitations are not discussed, such as reliance on known camera category tokens, behavior under incorrect camera-token selection, non-central camera models, rolling shutter, extreme calibration variation, outdoor scale changes, memory/runtime scaling with view count, and failure cases.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward multi-view geometry for fisheye and 360-degree imagery, where perspective-trained 3D foundation models are indeed brittle.

The overall formulation is plausible: combining a Pi3-style permutation-equivariant multi-view backbone with ray/radial decomposition, spherical-harmonic ray encoding, and camera-model conditioning is a reasonable direction for wide-FOV reconstruction.

The reported empirical gains over VGGT and Pi3 on raw wide-FOV inputs are large, especially for Stanford2D3D pose estimation and point-map reconstruction, suggesting that camera/model mismatch is a real failure mode for existing feed-forward methods.

The paper evaluates several relevant tasks: pose estimation, large-scale localization, point-map estimation, and monocular 360 depth, and includes ablations on camera tokens, camera-type training mixtures, and number of input frames.
weaknesses: The novelty is overstated. The main ingredients appear to be a combination of Pi3-style local/permutation-equivariant reconstruction, UniK3D-style ray/spherical-harmonic representation, and prompt/token conditioning. The paper does not convincingly isolate a new algorithmic insight beyond this integration, despite claiming a first foundation model for wide-FOV multi-view reconstruction.

The central claim of reconstruction without explicit calibration is not fully supported. A single camera-type token such as pinhole/fisheye/sphere cannot encode lens parameters, field of view, principal point, or camera-specific distortion variation. It is unclear how the method handles unseen fisheye lenses or arbitrary intrinsics, and the experiments do not adequately test this.

Evaluation fairness is a major concern. The main feed-forward baselines, VGGT and Pi3, are perspective-oriented and seem to be applied directly to distorted imagery. Stronger and more informative comparisons would include calibrated undistortion/rectification pipelines, omnidirectional SfM/MVS methods, and adaptations of the baselines with the same training data or camera augmentations.

The experimental protocol is underspecified. Dataset sizes, exact train/test splits, overlap with training datasets, number of scenes, sampling seeds, training iterations, SH degree, architecture details, token insertion mechanism, and compute budget are not sufficiently described for reproducibility. This is especially problematic because several evaluation datasets, such as Matterport3D and ScanNet++, are also listed among training datasets.

Some metrics and post-processing choices may mask errors. Point-map evaluation uses Umeyama alignment, MoGe optimal point alignment, and ICP sequentially, which can absorb scale, pose, and alignment mistakes. This makes it hard to tell whether the network predicts globally consistent geometry or whether evaluation-time registration is doing substantial work.

The pose evaluation is relatively weak despite strong reported numbers. RRA/RTA at 30 degrees is a loose threshold, Stanford2D3D uses only 20 sampled cases, and the paper does not report statistical confidence or sensitivity to sampling. The very large Stanford gains therefore need more careful validation.

The large-scale localization comparison is not convincingly presented. Wid3R is much faster, but its AUC is worse than EDM+IM360 on two of the three Matterport3D scenes, while the text claims superior registration accuracy. The comparison also mixes dense feed-forward prediction with SfM pipelines under different objectives and runtime/accuracy tradeoffs.

The ablation evidence is thin. The camera-token ablation shows only modest improvements, and the data-composition study has mixed results across accuracy/completion/normal consistency. It does not sufficiently establish that the proposed token mechanism, rather than extra training data and augmentation, is responsible for the gains.

Several technical details are unclear or potentially flawed, including the asymmetric ray loss notation, uncertainty supervision as an L1 match to residual magnitude, arccos losses without numerical-stability discussion, and how ray ground truth is obtained for all camera types. These issues make the method harder to assess and reproduce.

The limitation discussion is too narrow. Dynamic scenes are mentioned, but more central limitations are omitted: dependence on known camera category, lack of calibration-parameter generalization tests, possible dataset leakage, sensitivity to camera intrinsics, and reliance on heavy evaluation-time alignment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction methods such as VGGT and Pi3 largely assume perspective/pinhole inputs, while fisheye and 360-degree cameras are common in robotics, AR/VR, mapping, and egocentric capture.

The proposed formulation is technically plausible and well matched to the problem: decomposing prediction into ray direction and radial distance, using spherical-harmonic ray representations, and conditioning on camera-model tokens are sensible ways to make a shared architecture distortion-aware.

The empirical gains on wide-FOV settings are strong. The pose-estimation results on FIORD, Zip-NeRF, and especially Stanford2D3D show large improvements over VGGT and Pi3, and the point-map results similarly indicate clear robustness advantages on fisheye and 360-degree data.

The paper evaluates across several relevant tasks: pose estimation, point-map reconstruction, large-scale localization, monocular 360 depth, qualitative reconstructions, and ablations. This breadth supports the claim that the method is useful beyond a narrow benchmark.

The runtime comparison for large-scale 360 localization is compelling: a feed-forward model producing usable reconstructions in seconds is a meaningful systems advantage over dense matching plus SfM pipelines, even where accuracy is not uniformly best.

The ablation study is useful: it separately probes camera tokens, training data composition, and number of frames, and it supports the claim that cross-camera training and explicit camera conditioning help 360-degree generalization.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to Pi3 and UniK3D: the architecture appears to combine Pi3-style permutation-equivariant multi-view geometry with UniK3D-style spherical-harmonic ray modeling and camera conditioning. This is a strong engineering contribution, but the conceptual leap is moderate rather than foundational.

Some methodological details needed for reproducibility are underspecified, including the exact camera-token insertion mechanism, spherical-harmonic degree/order choices, training schedule and dataset sampling proportions, batch construction details, and how invalid/missing depth or ray supervision is handled across heterogeneous datasets.

The evaluation would be stronger with clearer discussion of training/test separation. Several benchmark datasets used for evaluation are also listed among the training datasets or are closely related to them, and the paper’s wording around Stanford2D3D in Table 7 versus earlier evaluation/training descriptions is confusing. This makes the strength of the zero-shot claim harder to assess.

The comparisons are not always fully apples-to-apples. Baselines such as VGGT and Pi3 are applied to wide-FOV images despite not being designed or trained for those camera models, while Wid3R is explicitly trained for them. That is a relevant practical comparison, but additional adapted or fine-tuned baselines would better isolate the contribution of the proposed representation.

The point-map evaluation uses a sequence of alignment steps including Umeyama, MoGe optimal point alignment, and ICP. While common in this area, these post-alignments can obscure absolute scale/pose errors, and the paper could better justify why this protocol fairly measures feed-forward reconstruction quality.

Some claims are slightly overstated. For example, in Matterport3D localization, Wid3R is much faster and registers all images, but it is not consistently the most accurate across all scenes and thresholds; the text sometimes reads stronger than the table supports.

The monocular 360 depth comparison is only partially convincing: Wid3R performs very well on delta accuracy but has worse AbsRel than several methods trained directly for panoramic depth. The paper correctly frames this as comparable, but the broader claim of superior monocular depth should be tempered.

The limitation section is narrow, focusing mainly on dynamic scenes. Other important limitations deserve discussion, such as dependence on known camera-model categories, behavior on unseen lens models, sensitivity to wrong camera tokens, memory/runtime scaling with many views, and failure cases under low overlap or moving objects.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in feed-forward 3D reconstruction: existing methods such as VGGT and pi3 largely assume perspective/pinhole inputs, while many robotics, AR/VR, and mapping settings use fisheye or 360 cameras. Supporting distorted wide-FoV imagery directly is a relevant ECCV contribution.

The proposed formulation is technically sensible: decomposing point-map prediction into angular ray prediction and radial distance prediction, using spherical-harmonic ray representation, and conditioning with camera-model tokens are natural adaptations of UniK3D-style ray modeling to multi-view reconstruction.

The experimental coverage is broad. The paper evaluates pose estimation, point-map estimation, large-scale localization, and monocular panoramic depth across fisheye and spherical datasets, with comparisons to feed-forward reconstruction models and several 360/localization baselines.

Results are generally strong, especially on 360-degree settings. The comparison to an in-house pi3 baseline trained with the same wide-angle data helps show that the ray-based modules and camera tokens add value beyond simply adding wide-FoV training data.
The supplementary material adds useful implementation and data details, including training dataset composition, sampling strategy, architecture variants, and additional qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental. The method combines a pi3-like multi-view backbone with UniK3D-like ray/radial decomposition and a categorical camera token. This is a reasonable engineering contribution, but the paper sometimes frames it more strongly than the conceptual advance supports.

Some claims are confounded by training data. Large gains over VGGT/pi3 often compare against models not trained on the same wide-FoV mixture, while the fairer Ours(pi3) baseline already closes much of the gap. The remaining gains are meaningful, especially for 360 data, but should be interpreted more narrowly.

The camera-model token is underspecified and potentially limiting. It appears to encode coarse known categories such as pinhole/fisheye/sphere rather than unknown continuous intrinsics or distortion parameters, so the claim of operating without explicit calibration is partly true but still relies on camera-type side information.

Evaluation choices may mask geometric errors. Point-map metrics apply Umeyama alignment, optimal point alignment, and ICP before scoring, which can make dense reconstruction quality difficult to disentangle from post-hoc alignment. More results without ICP or with stricter alignment protocols would strengthen the case.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main paper: the spherical harmonic degree/order, precise token design, training schedule, batch/image sampling settings, dataset split leakage safeguards, and compute/training duration are not fully specified.

The monocular depth comparison is mixed. Wid3R has strong delta accuracy but worse AbsRel than several dedicated 360-depth methods, so the claim of superior monocular depth performance should be softened to comparable performance under some metrics.

The limitation discussion is quite narrow, focusing mainly on dynamic scenes. Other important limitations, such as requiring known camera category, reduced benefits on some fisheye metrics, dependence on large supervised geometric datasets, and robustness to unseen lens models, deserve more direct discussion.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: feed-forward multi-view geometry for fisheye and 360-degree imagery, where pinhole-trained models such as VGGT and Pi3 often degrade.

The idea of decomposing reconstruction into ray direction and radial distance, while conditioning on camera model tokens, is a plausible adaptation of recent ray-based monocular geometry ideas to multi-view reconstruction.

The evaluation covers several relevant wide-FOV settings, including FIORD, Zip-NeRF, Matterport3D, Stanford2D3D, and ScanNet++, and reports pose, point-map, localization, and depth metrics rather than only one task.

The paper includes useful comparisons to both off-the-shelf feed-forward baselines and a retrained Pi3 variant using the authors' wide-angle training data, which helps separate some effects of data from architecture.
weaknesses: The central novelty is limited and somewhat overstated. The method appears to combine Pi3-style multi-view reconstruction with UniK3D-style ray/radial heads and a learned camera-category token. This is a reasonable engineering direction, but the paper repeatedly claims a first/general foundation model contribution without sufficiently distinguishing it from closely related ray-map, calibration-token, and omnidirectional geometry work.

The empirical evidence does not convincingly isolate the proposed contributions. The strongest gains over VGGT/Pi3 often come from training on a large composed wide-FOV dataset; the architecture gain over the authors' retrained Pi3 baseline is mixed, e.g. FIORD pose AUC is worse for Wid3R than Ours(Pi3), and some improvements are modest. The ablation does not cleanly separate ray representation, radial/angular heads, camera tokens, training data composition, and frame count.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness and reliability concerns. Several test sets are very small, such as 3 FIORD scenes, 4 Zip-NeRF scenes, 2 Stanford2D3D areas, and 3 Matterport3D localization scenes. Matterport3D and ScanNet++ are also used in training, but the paper does not clearly document split hygiene or possible scene overlap. Point-map metrics use multiple post-alignments including Umeyama, optimal point alignment, and ICP, which can hide pose/scale errors and make the feed-forward reconstruction claim harder to interpret.

The claims about operating without calibration or camera-specific preprocessing are not fully supported. Training uses ground-truth rays/depths and the model is given camera model tokens at inference. It is unclear how the method handles unknown camera models, varying intrinsics/distortion parameters within a camera family, or real calibration errors. A coarse token for pinhole/fisheye/sphere may not be enough to substantiate the broad camera-model generalization claim.

Several method details are underspecified or mathematically unclear. The spherical harmonics formulation does not specify the degree/order used, how coefficients vary spatially, or how unit-norm ray directions are enforced. The ray loss notation appears inconsistent, and key training details such as iterations, batch construction, sampling probabilities, compute budget, and exact model sizes are insufficient for reproducibility.

Some results are presented in an overly favorable way. For monocular 360 depth, Wid3R has high delta1.25 but much worse AbsRel than several specialized methods, yet the text frames performance as comparable or superior. The reported percentage improvements in the abstract can be misleading because they mix absolute metric changes and relative percentages over weak baselines.

The paper would benefit from stronger baselines and stress tests, such as calibrated cubemap/perspective pipelines with matched compute, classical omnidirectional SfM under the same data selection, robustness to wrong camera tokens, unseen distortion parameters, cross-dataset generalization with no target-dataset training, and evaluation on dynamic or outdoor wide-FOV sequences.

Presentation and reproducibility are below the standard expected for a convincing ECCV submission. The paper includes unclear table formatting, missing project URL content, odd figure/icon choices, and limited discussion of failure cases. These issues are secondary to the technical concerns but further reduce confidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction methods such as VGGT and pi3 are largely designed around perspective/pinhole imagery, while fisheye and 360-degree cameras are common in robotics, AR/VR, navigation, and mapping. The problem is well motivated and clearly relevant to ECCV.

The core design is sensible: decomposing reconstruction into angular ray prediction and radial distance estimation, using spherical-harmonic ray representations, and conditioning on camera-model tokens is a coherent way to adapt feed-forward reconstruction to wide-FoV imagery. The method builds on strong recent foundations while making a practical extension that appears useful.

The experimental evidence is broad and mostly convincing. The paper evaluates pose estimation, point-map estimation, large-scale localization, and monocular 360 depth across fisheye and spherical datasets including FIORD, Zip-NeRF, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and Stanford2D3D. Wid3R shows large gains over unadapted VGGT/pi3 and also improves over a pi3 variant trained with the same wide-angle data in most key 360-degree settings.

The ablations are meaningful. The comparisons of camera-token conditioning, training data composition, number of frames, and radial-module attention help support the claims that both the ray-based formulation and explicit camera conditioning matter, rather than all improvements coming solely from extra training data.

The paper is generally clear and reproducible at the level expected for a conference submission: it reports training datasets, augmentations, losses, evaluation splits, metrics, and implementation details. The supplementary material adds useful architecture and data configuration details.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental in architectural terms. Much of the method is a combination of pi3-style permutation-equivariant multi-view reconstruction and UniK3D-style ray/angular-radial modeling, with camera-model tokens added as conditioning. This is a strong and useful integration, but the paper should more sharply distinguish what is technically new beyond combining these ingredients.

The claim of operating without explicit calibration needs nuance. The method does not require per-image calibration at inference, but it does require the camera model category/token and is trained with ground-truth ray/depth/pose supervision derived from known camera geometry. The paper sometimes presents this as more calibration-free than the evidence strictly supports.

Some comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. The strongest improvements over VGGT and pi3 partly reflect that those baselines were not designed or trained for distorted wide-FoV data, while the 'Ours (pi3)' adaptation is often a much stronger baseline. On FIORD pose AUC, for example, the wide-data pi3 variant is better than Wid3R, and in large-scale localization Wid3R is much faster but not uniformly more accurate than SfM-based methods such as EDM+IM360.

The point-map evaluation uses a sequence of Umeyama alignment, optimal point alignment, and ICP, which may obscure errors in scale, pose, or global consistency. Since one of the main claims is feed-forward reconstruction quality, additional metrics before ICP or with stricter alignment would make the evidence more transparent.

The ablation on camera-model tokens is useful but not exhaustive. It would be valuable to test confusion or robustness when the wrong token is supplied, when camera types are unseen or intermediate, or when lens parameters vary substantially within a camera category. This matters because a discrete token may not capture continuous distortion variation.

Some writing and notation issues reduce polish: several equations have formatting artifacts, the ray loss notation is hard to parse, the uncertainty loss is only lightly justified, and the supplementary section on panorama-based scene generation is speculative and not integrated into the main empirical case. These are fixable but currently make parts of the paper less crisp.
